title: How Monster Trucks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how monster trucks work, starting with their off-roading roots and Bob Chandler's 1979 Bigfoot, the first monster truck. They cover the early Bigfoot promotions and imitators, the shift from modified pickups to purpose-built tubular chrome-moly roll cages, mid-engine layouts and fiberglass bodies that are swapped between shows, freestyle tricks like backflips popularized by Dennis Anderson's Grave Digger, the blown methanol "alky" engines, long-travel nitrogen shocks and low-pressure tires, driver safety (strapped-in head restraints, kill switches, spectator safety), Feld Entertainment's takeover of Monster Jam, and a listener correction about uranium and the Big Bang.

entities.name: Take This Job and Shove It

segments.title: Opening banter and off-roading stories
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the show's date and monster truck announcers, then Chuck recounts his father's off-roading in Jeeps and a jump with no seatbelts. Josh admits he has never been off-roading or to a monster truck show.

segments.title: Monster truck events and terminology
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the noise and atmosphere of monster truck events, stadium versus indoor venues, and whether to call them rallies, jams, or cotillions. They note that Monster Jam is a specific brand.

segments.title: Bob Chandler and the first Bigfoot
segments.summary: Bob Chandler, an aggressive off-road driver from St. Louis, upgraded his truck and opened the Midwest Four Wheel Drive Center. His 1979 truck, Bigfoot, used 44-inch tires and four-wheel steering, and he is widely credited as the inventor of the monster truck. A reported ticket for high headlights is mentioned as unverified.

segments.title: Bigfoot promotions, imitators and early shows
segments.summary: Bigfoot toured doing promotional events, crushing cars in slow motion. Its popularity spawned imitators who performed at car shows and drag races, and a second Bigfoot debuted in 1982 at the Pontiac Silverdome on 66-inch tires. The hosts discuss the agricultural tires and tread shaving.

segments.title: From modified pickups to purpose-built chrome-moly trucks
segments.summary: Early monster trucks were modified pickups such as F-250s and Chevrolets, which broke axles. Chandler and a group moved to purpose-built frames made of lightweight chrome-moly tubing (Chrome Moly) in the late 1980s, creating a tubular roll cage, with the engine moved behind the driver and fiberglass bodies.

segments.title: Body swapping, backflips and the Anderson family
segments.summary: Crews swap fiberglass bodies between shows to reduce transport, since multiple trucks often share a body. The hosts describe single and consecutive backflips. Dennis Anderson's Grave Digger and his family are discussed, with his push toward freestyle tricks and Kristen Anderson's 33-foot-9-inch jump record.

segments.title: Engines, methanol fuel and suspension
segments.summary: Monster trucks are about 9,000 to 12,000 pounds, built light for speed. They use supercharged, blown methanol (alky) engines with two gears. Methanol allows more power when blown, and the Raminator reportedly got 264 feet per gallon. Each wheel has nitrogen-charged shocks with about 24 inches of travel, and tires run at 8 to 10 psi.

segments.title: Driver safety, cockpit design and spectator danger
segments.summary: The hosts describe the center-seat driver position, head-restraint style immobilization, ratcheted five-point harnesses, molded seats, and the need for physical fitness. They cover fire suppression, spectator injuries and deaths, the lower seating kept empty, and remote kill switches held by crew members.

segments.title: Bigfoot variants, Feld takeover and closing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the many Bigfoot trucks, including Bigfoot 5 with very tall tires, and fun body designs such as Grave Digger, El Toro Loco and Zombie Chuck. They describe the Feld Entertainment takeover of Monster Jam, rigged outcomes, Bob Chandler's absence from Monster Jam, and wrap up with a listener correction about uranium and the Big Bang.
